concept: Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity

claims.text: Figma distinguishes user flows, which map user actions and decisions, from task flows focused on a single action and wireframes focused on interface layout and structure. These artifacts answer different design questions. (low confidence)

A wireframe can make screen structure and layout testable without finished visual details. It should not be interpreted as evidence about every visual attribute of a finished interface. (medium confidence)

For the boundary between flow diagrams and detailed specifications, practitioner Michael Lai proposes high-level task flows plus annotated detailed designs for deviations or new interaction patterns, so developers can resolve questions without detailing every familiar interaction. (low confidence)

In a UX Stack Exchange practitioner account, leaving error states and secondary screens until high-fidelity prototyping led to missing screens and user dead ends. The author later reported that covering error flows in wireframes saved team effort; this is an experience report, not a measured universal effect. (low confidence)

Walker, Takayama and Landay found few differences in the number, type and severity of usability issues across paper/computer and low/high-fidelity website prototypes in their experiment. MeasuringU’s review likewise supports low-fidelity prototypes for finding major issues, while warning they are imperfect substitutes. This supports early issue discovery, not equivalence for every test outcome. (medium confidence)

GOV.UK warns that an online alpha prototype cannot support the full range of technical accessibility tests used for production code. Prototype findings therefore leave a specific validation boundary for the later implementation. (low confidence)

Figma recommends defining the user goal, entry point, meaningful steps, decision points and success endpoint. Its decision-point guidance explicitly includes error messages and alternative paths, so a flow should represent relevant exceptions rather than only a successful route. (low confidence)

Scope prototypes around learning: GOV.UK advises focusing alpha prototypes on the most challenging areas to test risky assumptions, rather than necessarily building the entire journey. Ontario describes alpha as testing hypotheses and trying approaches with users before building a service. (medium confidence)

GOV.UK recommends code prototypes for realistic service interactions, but says prototype code need not meet production security or traffic-performance standards and must not simply be copied into production. Its alpha guidance similarly calls for testing code rather than production-quality implementation. (medium confidence)

GOV.UK recommends code prototypes for realistic service research; Walker and colleagues found low- and high-fidelity prototypes equally good at uncovering usability issues in their experiment. The positions address different scopes: realistic interaction versus issue discovery in the tested websites. Neither establishes that one fidelity is best for every research question. (low confidence)

Fidelity has separable dimensions such as interaction, visual appearance and content. Presentation medium is also a separate choice: paper versus computer should not be treated as equivalent to low versus high fidelity. (medium confidence)

Pilot a prototype before study sessions. NN/G warns that a wrong screen or slow simulated response can alter user expectations and interpretation; when an action has no prepared response, it recommends asking what the participant expected rather than explaining how the design should work. (low confidence)
NN/g treats fidelity as separable dimensions of interactivity, visuals, and content or commands. A prototype can be detailed in one dimension and rough in another. (low confidence)

Task-based prototype evaluation can observe people performing typical product tasks and use their mistakes and comments to find usability problems. Figma also recommends using user flows to guide test scenarios and the important steps to evaluate. (medium confidence)

Do not assume prototype timings or appearance ratings predict the finished product. A mobile-phone experiment reported possible overestimation of task completion time with a computer prototype and inflated aesthetic judgments for reduced-fidelity prototypes; MeasuringU’s review also finds weaker accuracy for task times and aesthetic measures. (medium confidence)

NN/g distinguishes clickable prototypes, whose action responses are prepared before testing, from static prototypes, whose responses a person supplies during testing. Pilot the prototype: NN/g warns that operator errors can affect the study. (low confidence)
Treat a prototype as a candidate design hypothesis: observe people using it, compare approaches and revise or discard ideas before committing to a build. (medium confidence)

Choose prototype detail and medium to fit the research question and practical constraints. Sketches can explore basic ideas; more realistic code or interactive prototypes support tests of realistic interactions. A mandatory paper-to-polished sequence is not established by these sources. (medium confidence)

For inclusive interaction testing, the GOV.UK Prototype Kit guidance identifies code prototypes as a way to test on the user’s own device and with assistive technology such as a screen reader; it also supports branching based on user input. The medium must support the interaction being investigated. (medium confidence)

Walker, Takayama and Landay’s controlled web-prototype experiment found no significant difference in the number or severity of usability issues across fidelity or paper/computer conditions, but did find differences in issue types by fidelity. This supports using low fidelity for some formative testing without assuming identical findings. (low confidence)

Advice about fidelity and willingness to criticize is qualified: NN/G argues that unfinished-looking prototypes can encourage negative feedback, whereas MeasuringU reports a study finding participants just as likely to offer critiques on paper and high-fidelity computer prototypes. Do not treat increased criticism from low fidelity as universal. (low confidence)
